podcasts.title: Taking on ServiceNow: Coding Agents the Rest of Us with Serval Co-Founder and CEO Jake Stauch
podcasts.transcript: This is the ultimate moonshot in enterprise software. These agents that go off and do work for you and magically discover all your problems and solve all your problems. And I think no one's really figured out how to do this well. >> This is kind of the open AI hugging face incidents or other things where agents are given a task and then they do something that's unexpected. The agent becomes pretty competent. They could theoretically just start writing code that could take action on your systems. And that is an unbounded security risk that I don't think anyone's going to be able to take anytime soon. On the one hand, you want these to be very autonomous without somebody babysitting them. On the other hand, autonomy is very scary in the enterprise. Servil is the boundary. Servil is the guardrails. We are the way that a large enterprise with a lot of rules and approvals and process and politics can adopt these tools safely and comfortably at scale. Hi listeners, welcome back to No Priors. Today Allah and I are here with Jake Stouch, co-founder and CEO of Serville. Servil with all the speed of the African wildcat is trying to attack service now and more broadly bringing the power of code generation to IT and enterprise teams overall. Welcome Jake. >> Jake, thanks for joining us today on No Prior. >> Great. Great to be here. >> Yeah, maybe you could tell us a little bit more about your history and how you started Serval and what what is the problem that you started with or why did you start working on this to begin with? >> Yeah, so background serval is enterprise automation, enterprise service management. The idea is you can ask questions and get help at work and automate a lot of the parts of the job you don't enjoy and we do that through codegen agents. So that's the what the company does. We compete with companies like Service Now is historically the big legacy provider in the space. I discovered this category actually working at a previous company called Vicata uh where we sold enterprise physical security products to IT teams. Spent many many years talking to IT teams figuring out what to build for them. And one of the things I love to to do with these teams is ask them what do you spend the most money on and what do you hate the most? And Service Now would top a lot of those lists. And so I was always interested in this category of maybe there's a better solution here, but it wasn't clear for most of my time there how you'd ever beat Service Now. They're a great company. They've done so much so well and why would you be able to compete with them? >> What was frustrating for users about it? >> I think so hard to build in the platform. So it's a very robust, customizable, powerful platform that can map to all these enterprise workflows, fundamentally it's a workflow automation platform. And so it can do so much, but every idea you have for doing something cool, you have to go and implement. And a lot of times you're bringing in consultants to implement it. So it it's always kind of running 6 to 12 months behind where you want it to be. And it's fine if you're building something that's going to last 5 10 years like a big onboarding flow and nothing about your business is going to change. So you can invest all that upfront effort and then it gets deployed and it works for a while. but for just trying to keep up with all the automation that you want to build. Service Now is not able to catch up and and then it's very expensive and it keeps getting more expensive over time. So that frustration of it's not keeping up with where I want to go as a business and it keeps getting more expensive. That's what was driving a lot of the frustration. I think one thing that you mentioned that's really interesting about what you do is if you look at the world of AI adoption, a lot of the really early adoption is coding agents. Yes. And that's engineers using it to build applications for their business or products or other things. And what you folks have been doing is really pioneering expansion of the category in terms of saying we should let anybody internally an IT person etc. build internal products or tools that can be used broadly across the enterprise. You're basically providing like coding agents for for the all the internal stuff. >> Yeah. >> Uh for people who often aren't that adept at coding. So can you talk more about that? I think it's like super fascinating. >> Yeah. I love this idea of coding agents for the rest of us because if you think so much of the early enterprise adoption in AI has been engineering teams and you think about why that is there's a lot of reasons obviously early adopters in a lot of different technologies but also they're able to build and experiment with these tools because they have this process of code review it's very safe for even a 19-year-old intern to build something very powerful and then go through this process before it goes into production we want to bring that same capability to the rest of the enterprise so we build a platform that brings coding agents to IT departments who then can bring it to HR and finance and people teams and legal teams and they can do it because under the hood it's coding agents but then you have all these abstractions and guard rails and controls. So things go through approval, they go through a staging and uh approval cycle and audit trail and all of that. And so it's how do you build a system that makes it easy for everyone to be a builder. And the core insight here was that it actually wants to build stuff. And for most of the world they don't have an engineering department. They have an IT department. Most companies have an IT department. not not a team of software engineers and so it is what's building and configuring technology for the company and we're building essentially the AI platform for them. How does how does that run into things like all the different more like workforce agents that are being developed like dot from open AI or you know some of these things where you almost have a virtual assistant that will go and do things for you. Yeah, I think those really work well for consumers and SMB and even a lot of the mid-market organizations in a large enterprise. There's so much and I didn't even really appreciate this going in. There is so much process around approvals around what you can and can't do. The permission sets of any individual are so limited that even if you were allowed to bring your agent to work, which a lot of cases you're not, what it can what it can do is so incredibly limited it can it can barely even read your emails. Um, and so when you think about all the stuff you need to do at work and all the systems you want to touch and all the interesting automations you could build, your personal permissions end up being so limited that these personal agents are also incredibly limited and all not all that useful. You're kind of taking that and putting it in the hands directly of the IT department. Are you also exploring this more forward sort of forward deployed motion or how do you actually get this really built out in the enterprise or used effectively? >> Yeah, absolutely. Um at the beginning did you think you were going to do that? I think that that actually >> a lot of people would have started with like you know automation on top of their ticketing system for example. >> Exactly. And these drag and drop workflow builders is a painful level of abstraction because it's too complex for nontechnical users and it's annoyingly abstracted for technical users. And so from a workflow automation perspective, we thought it would get there. In the early days, it did not. So what we ended up doing in all our early demos, we would prompt the LLM and say, "Hey, here's a suggested way you might want to build a password reset workflow." And so we'd we we'd seed it with like a lot of examples and then over time we'd make that library bigger and bigger, but then the models just got so good that eventually it became hard to break. It became hard for you to give it a workflow that it couldn't automate if the APIs existed. >> Yeah. >> When you think about where coding agents are today and what your customers want, like what are you are you and Alex excited about them getting better from here? Are you nervous? like what do you think it looks like uh in terms of impact on your own product? >> We are so excited for them to get better because I think it unlocks a lot of the things that we'd love to do around you know better browser use and computer use and more of a approach to background agents and personal agents that can be really useful in the enterprise. So we're excited for the evolution of the category. We've always believed fundamentally that we are not building the LMS ourselves. Um we are building the guard rails. The intelligence getting better just makes our product more powerful and also makes our customers want to actually clamp down even further on those boundaries on those guardrails. And and we're seeing this in cyber security risk right now. >> Absolutely. >> And and so what I'm actually going to want to do if I'm a large enterprise is shrink everyone's permissions down to truly lease privilege.
